newsReadings.title: A Warming Climate Threatens Italy's Prized White Truffles
newsReadings.source: Associated Press, 'From Italy to Croatia, a warming climate threatens prized white truffles,' 1 November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
In the wooded hills around Alba, in northern Italy, the white truffle season traditionally begins on 1 October, when hunters known as trifolau set out with their dogs before dawn. This year, however, the ritual has been shadowed by anxiety. Months of heat and drought have left soils dry and compacted, and the prized fungus — which depends on cool, moist earth and a delicate symbiotic relationship with the roots of oak, hazel and poplar trees — has emerged smaller, scarcer, and with a shorter shelf life. For a region whose identity and economy are bound up with this seasonal treasure, a poor harvest is not merely a culinary disappointment; it is a warning about a changing climate.

The white truffle, Tuber magnatum, cannot be cultivated in the way that ordinary mushrooms can. It grows underground, exchanging nutrients with host trees through a network of fungal threads, and it fruits only when soil temperature, moisture and the surrounding microbial community align. Researchers explain that prolonged summer heat disrupts this alignment: dry soils crack and harden, the fine roots on which the fungus depends retreat, and the aroma compounds that give the truffle its value develop less fully. Antonio Degiacomi, president of Italy's National Centre for Truffle Studies, has described an October characterised by poor production and poor keeping quality, a direct consequence of the rainless July and August that preceded it.

The consequences extend well beyond the dinner table. Alba's annual truffle fair draws visitors from around the world, and the surrounding forests support a web of livelihoods — hunters, restaurateurs, hoteliers, and traders who grade and auction the finest specimens for sums that can reach thousands of euros per kilogram. When the harvest contracts, prices rise sharply, tempting counterfeiters and putting pressure on honest producers. More profoundly, the truffle's plight illustrates a broader ecological principle: species that depend on narrow, stable conditions are among the first to register environmental change, acting as indicators of stresses that will eventually affect less celebrated organisms, from soil microbes to the trees themselves.

Scientists and forest managers are responding on several fronts. One approach is improved forest management: protecting mature woodland, limiting soil compaction from machinery and foot traffic, and preserving the mixed-age tree cover that keeps forest floors shaded and humid. Another is experimental irrigation during prolonged droughts, an attempt, in the words of one researcher, to do artificially what nature does on its own — to keep the soil environment within the range the fungus requires. A third line of inquiry looks underground, studying soil microorganisms and searching for tree varieties better suited to hotter and drier conditions, in the hope that future forests will be more resilient even as the climate warms.

The human knowledge embedded in the hunt is itself at risk. A trained dog learns to distinguish the scent of a ripe truffle from the many other fungi in the forest floor, and an experienced hunter learns to read subtle signs — the moisture of the soil, the species and age of nearby trees, the slope and shade of a hillside — that indicate where fruiting is most likely. That expertise is passed down through families and local associations, not written in textbooks, and a succession of poor seasons threatens the apprenticeship on which it depends, as younger hunters question whether a livelihood so exposed to weather can sustain them.

None of these measures offers a guarantee. The researchers involved are careful to distinguish adaptation from rescue: forests can be managed, but they cannot be insulated from a climate that continues to warm, and irrigation is expensive, water-intensive, and difficult to scale across rugged terrain. What the truffle story does offer is clarity. It shows, in a single, tangible commodity, how abstract projections of rising temperatures translate into concrete losses — smaller harvests, higher prices, and a tradition under strain. Whether future generations will still gather in Alba each autumn to celebrate the white truffle may depend less on the skill of the hunters and their dogs than on the willingness of societies to protect the forests, soils and climates on which such traditions quietly depend.

questions.q: Why is the white truffle particularly vulnerable to heat and drought?
options: Because it is harvested only in winter.
Because it depends on cool, moist soils and a symbiotic relationship with tree roots.
Because it grows on the surface of leaves.
Because hunters refuse to search in hot weather.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did the president of Italy's National Centre for Truffle Studies describe?
options: An October characterised by poor production and poor keeping quality after a rainless July and August.
The discovery of a new truffle species.

questions.q: The passage presents the truffle as an ecological indicator because species with narrow, stable requirements:
options: Are among the first to register environmental change.
Do not interact with other organisms.

What limitation of irrigation does the passage note?
options: It is expensive, water-intensive, and difficult to scale across rugged terrain.
It makes truffles grow too large.
It is banned by the truffle fair.

newsReadings.title: Fewer Deals, Bigger Bets: Climate Tech in Autumn 2026
newsReadings.source: InnovationZero, 'Fewer deals, bigger bets: climate tech in autumn 2026,' autumn 2026 (first-half reports from Currence, Net Zero Insights and Sightline Climate)
newsReadings.passage:
Climate technology investment in 2026 presents a paradox: the headline sums are larger than ever, yet the number of companies receiving funding has fallen to a record low. According to first-half reports from analysts including Currence, Net Zero Insights and Sightline Climate, climate venture funding reached $26.1 billion in the first six months of the year, up 55 per cent on the same period a year earlier, even as the deal count dropped by roughly a quarter. The explanation is concentration: rounds of $100 million or more absorbed about 65 per cent of all funding, and the average round rose to around $27 million. In other words, investors are making fewer bets, but much bigger ones.

The most striking shift concerns where the money goes. Low-carbon data centres accounted for 34 per cent of global climate venture funding, up from just 3 per cent a year earlier, as the artificial intelligence boom drives demand for electricity that is clean, firm, and available quickly. A report produced by Currence with HSBC found developers willing to pay up to $150 per megawatt-hour for such power, against a benchmark of about $100, a premium that reflects how urgently computing capacity must be built. Geothermal and nuclear companies have benefited most visibly: Fervo's $1.9 billion geothermal listing and X-energy's $1.0 billion nuclear listing set records for their sectors, suggesting that public markets, too, are rewarding technologies that can deliver power around the clock.

Not every corner of climate technology has shared in the boom. Funding for carbon removal fell 61 per cent to its lowest level since 2020, and low-carbon fuels dropped 56 per cent, after Microsoft paused purchases of new carbon removal credits in the spring — a decision that reverberated through a market heavily dependent on a small number of large buyers. Founders surveyed by CTVC and Elemental Impact named capital structure as their biggest financing challenge, with 43 per cent saying access to project capital had worsened over the past year, against 32 per cent who said it had improved. For companies that must build physical plants rather than merely write software, the gap between a promising prototype and a bankable project remains the hardest to cross.

The geography of fundraising has also shifted. Europe leads in raising new climate funds, but the United States raises far more for its own companies, and the United Kingdom has slipped to third place behind China in fund formation. Meanwhile, Sightline Climate's survey of dry powder — capital committed to funds but not yet invested — shows record fundraising in 2025, with $92 billion closed across 179 funds, of which infrastructure funds captured 77 per cent of new capital. Venture capital, by contrast, now attracts under 8 per cent of new climate fund capital. The industry, in short, is tilting away from early-stage risk towards large, asset-heavy projects whose revenues are easier to model.

What does this concentration mean for the energy transition itself? Optimists argue that scale is precisely what is needed: data centres, geothermal plants and grid infrastructure require enormous sums, and channelling capital towards proven approaches may accelerate emissions cuts faster than scattering it across hundreds of speculative start-ups. Sceptics counter that today's winners may entrench a narrow vision of decarbonisation, while neglected areas — carbon removal, sustainable fuels, adaptation for vulnerable communities — struggle to attract the patient capital they need. Earth observation funding, which tripled on the back of a $521 million round for ICEYE, hints at a middle path: investors are increasingly paying to measure physical climate risk as it materialises, rather than merely to prevent it. The autumn of 2026 may therefore be remembered less for how much was invested than for how decisively investors chose where the future would be built.

questions.q: What paradox does the passage identify in 2026 climate technology investment?
options: Funding rose sharply while the number of funded companies fell to a record low.
Funding fell while the number of deals rose.
No climate companies received any funding.
All funding went to a single company.

questions.q: According to the passage, low-carbon data centres accounted for what share of global climate venture funding?
Why did carbon removal funding fall sharply, according to the passage?
options: Because the technology was proven impossible.
Because Microsoft paused purchases of new carbon removal credits, hitting a market dependent on few large buyers.
Because data centres replaced all other technologies.

questions.q: What does the passage say about the geography of climate fundraising?
options: Europe leads in raising funds, but the US raises far more for its own companies, and the UK has slipped behind China.
China raises no climate funds at all.
The UK leads the world in fund formation.
All fundraising now takes place in the United States.

questions.q: The sceptical view presented in the final paragraph is that concentration may:
options: Guarantee emissions cuts in every sector.
Entrench a narrow vision of decarbonisation while neglected areas struggle for capital.
Eliminate the need for infrastructure investment.

questions.q: The passage states that climate venture funding reached $26.1 billion in the first half of 2026.
The passage states that venture capital now attracts more than half of new climate fund capital.
